bodyHtml:
Everything in this track depends on the data. A volume profile is only as good as the volume it counts, and a footprint only as good as its record of who was the aggressor. This chapter explains where real volume comes from, why spot forex doesn't have it, what tick volume is and isn't, and what the main platforms say about how they build their order-flow tools. It stays neutral: Stryker has no affiliate relationship with any platform named here, and nothing below is a recommendation to buy one.

Why futures have real volume

A futures contract like ES trades on one exchange, CME Globex, through one central order book. Every order and every trade passes through the same matching engine (VP-07). That means the exchange's data feed is a complete record: every contract traded, at what price, and whether it hit the bid or lifted the ask. CME's market-by-order feed goes further, showing each individual resting order, anonymously. That completeness is what makes volume profile and footprint analysis meaningful on futures.

Why spot FX doesn't

Spot forex is an over-the-counter (OTC) market. There is no central exchange. Trades happen between banks, brokers, electronic platforms and their clients across the world. The Bank for International Settlements' triennial survey measured global FX trading at about $7.5 trillion a day in April 2022, and that figure comes from a survey of dealers, not from a tape. No single feed sees all of it.

So when your forex broker's chart shows a "volume" bar, it can't be the market's volume. It is usually one of two things: the broker's own trade count, or tick volume.

Tick volume: what it is and isn't

Tick volume counts how many times the price changed during a bar, not how many contracts or units traded. It is a measure of activity. Busy periods produce more price changes, so tick volume often rises and falls with real activity. That is why some traders use it as a stand-in.

The problem is size. A tick that moved price after one small order and a tick that moved it after a huge one count the same. The illustrative data shows the typical pattern: the direction of the two series mostly agrees, but the proportions don't. A volume profile built from tick volume shows where price changed most often, which is not the same thing as where the most business was done. Footprints and delta built from spot FX quotes have the same weakness and can't know who was the aggressor.

The practical answer for FX traders is to use the currency futures instead. CME lists Euro FX futures (6E) and other currency futures with exchange-reported volume. Many traders build their EUR/USD profile on 6E and apply the levels to spot, accepting that the prices differ slightly (futures include the interest-rate difference between the two currencies). The same logic applies to gold: GC futures have real volume; spot XAU/USD from a CFD broker does not.

The contracts this track uses

From CME's contract specifications and Micro E-mini FAQ:

Micro contracts (MES, MNQ) share their big brothers' prices and ticks but are one tenth the size. Their volume is separate, so a profile built on MES shows MES volume only. Most order-flow traders read the full-size contract (ES, NQ) for the data, even if they trade the micro.

Contract months and rolls

Futures expire. ES and NQ are quarterly (March, June, September, December). CME's roll-date page says the customary roll is the Monday before the third Friday of the expiry month, and that after it the next contract becomes the "lead month" because the expiring one grows less liquid. For 2026 the U.S. index roll dates are 16 March, 15 June, 14 September and 14 December.

This matters for profiles. Around the roll, volume moves from one contract to the other, so a composite that mixes the two months, or a continuous chart that splices them, can show a volume shelf that is really just the roll. Continuous contracts may also be back-adjusted to remove the price gap between months, which moves every historic level. When you carry levels across a roll, check which method your platform uses.

The platforms, in their own words

The table below summarises what each platform's own documentation says about its order-flow and profile tools. Features and prices change, and several need a paid data feed or subscription for real-time futures data, so check the current details yourself.

Sierra Chart

Footprint / order flow: Numbers Bars (bid x ask, delta, cumulative delta).

Volume profile / TPO: Volume by Price; TPO profile charts.

Notes from its own documentation: Numbers Bars need only best bid/ask with each trade, not full depth.

NinjaTrader 8

Footprint / order flow: Order Flow Volumetric Bars (imbalances, delta, cumulative delta).

Volume profile / TPO: Volume profile tools.

Notes from its own documentation: Imbalance compared diagonally; default ratio 1.5.

ATAS

Footprint / order flow: Cluster (footprint) charts; imbalance settings.

Volume profile / TPO: Volume profile tools.

Notes from its own documentation: Default imbalance 200%, strong 400%, adjustable.

Bookmap

Footprint / order flow: Order-book heatmap and trade bubbles; add-ons for icebergs and stops.

Volume profile / TPO: Volume profile add-ons.

Notes from its own documentation: Iceberg detection works only from CME MBO data.

TradingView

Footprint / order flow: Volume Footprint (on paid plans).

Volume profile / TPO: Session, fixed-range, visible-range profiles; TPO.

Notes from its own documentation: Footprint classifies buys/sells from intrabar price moves, not exchange aggressor tags.

Two differences matter most. The first is how buys and sells are classified. Tools that use the exchange's bid and ask at the time of each trade (Sierra Chart, NinjaTrader, ATAS, Bookmap on futures feeds) give true aggressor-side delta. TradingView's footprint uses intrabar price direction, which is an approximation. The second is depth of data: iceberg and individual-order tools need market-by-order data; footprints only need trades with the best bid and ask.

What even perfect futures data can't tell you

Complete exchange data is a big advantage, but it has limits worth stating plainly.

  • It is anonymous. CME's market-by-order feed identifies orders by anonymous IDs only. You never know who traded, so words like "institutions" or "smart money" in order-flow commentary are interpretations, not data.
  • It shows one venue. ES is closely linked to the S&P 500 stocks, their options, and ETFs that track the index. Large participants may be active in several of those at once. The ES footprint shows only the ES part.
  • It can't see intentions. Resting orders can be cancelled, and orders not yet sent don't exist in any feed.
  • Aggressor is not direction. A trade at the ask may be a new long or a short covering. The data does not say which.

None of this makes order flow useless. It means the right claim is modest: order-flow tools show how trading happened at a price, which is valuable context at a level you already care about. They don't reveal a hidden plan.

A note on cost and simulation

Real-time exchange data is licensed, so most platforms charge for live CME feeds separately from the software, and non-professional and professional data are priced differently. You don't need any of it to learn. Several platforms offer replay of historical sessions or simulated trading, and the exercises in this track can all be done on delayed or recorded data. Pay for live data once you know which tools you actually use.

Worked example: checking your own setup

  1. Instrument: are you looking at an exchange-traded future (ES, NQ, GC, CL, 6E) or a broker's CFD or spot price?
  2. Volume type: does your platform say "volume" (contracts) or "tick volume"? Check its documentation, not the label on the chart.
  3. Delta method: is the buy/sell split from exchange bid/ask, or from price direction?
  4. Session: RTH or overnight (VP-05)?
  5. Contract: front month or continuous, and is it back-adjusted?

For a futures trader, a typical set of answers might read: ES front month, contract volume, exchange bid/ask delta, RTH session, front month only with no back-adjustment. For a forex trader it might read: 6E front month for profiles, spot EUR/USD for execution, and no footprint reading on spot at all.

Write the answers at the top of your playbook. If two traders disagree about where yesterday's POC was, one of these five is almost always why.

Common mistakes

  • Reading a footprint on spot FX or a CFD as if it showed real aggressor volume.
  • Building a profile on micro-contract volume and comparing it with someone else's ES profile.
  • Ignoring the roll when building composites across expiry.
  • Assuming all delta is the same. Exchange bid/ask and tick-rule methods can disagree.
  • Buying a platform before you know what you need. Most offer trials or simulated data.

Key takeaways

  • Futures trade through one central book, so their volume and aggressor data are complete.
  • Spot FX is OTC with no single tape; broker "volume" is usually tick volume.
  • Tick volume counts price changes. It tracks activity, not size.
  • Use currency and gold futures for FX and gold profile work.
  • Know how your platform classifies buys and sells, and watch for roll effects.

Practice exercises

  1. Put a 6E futures chart next to a spot EUR/USD chart for the same day. Compare the session profiles' POCs.
  2. Find out whether your platform's volume on spot instruments is tick volume. Quote the line from its documentation.
  3. Build a 20-day ES composite that crosses a roll date, then rebuild it on the front month only. Note what changes.
  4. Answer the five setup questions from the worked example and save them in your playbook.

Self-check quiz

1. Why does ES have complete volume data?

Every trade goes through CME Globex's single central order book, which publishes it.

2. What does tick volume count?

The number of price changes in a bar, not the size traded.

3. How can an FX trader get real volume for EUR/USD?

Use CME Euro FX futures (6E), which have exchange-reported volume.

4. When is the customary roll date for U.S. equity index futures?

The Monday before the third Friday of the expiry month.

5. How does TradingView's footprint classify buys and sells?

From intrabar price direction, which approximates aggressor side.
